title: Caching and the Cost of Remembering
html:
During a promotion, forty thousand customers opened the same product page on Baodium. The product description, category, and image references were unchanged across most requests, yet the original Catalog read path fetched those fields from the database each time. Each query was quick. At that request volume, the repeated reads occupied a large share of available database connections.

The Catalog team proposed reusing previously retrieved values for subsequent requests. The reduction in database traffic was easy to estimate, but the design also had to specify how long a value remained acceptable, which source updates invalidated it, and how many direct database reads could execute when the cache was empty or unavailable.

The admission limits from Chapter 4 still apply when a cache misses. They become especially important after many cached entries expire together, or when the cache itself fails and concurrent requests attempt to read directly from the database.

Repeated Reads and Reusable Results

The affected Product Page Service instance normally handled about 1,200 page requests per second. Each page fetched product metadata, category information, and image references, producing 3,600 database reads per second. Promotional traffic increased that rate to approximately 4,320. Figure Figure shows what repeated reads do to a pool.

Those reads used a pool of 40 connections. At eight milliseconds of mean connection occupancy, the promotional workload accounted for about 34.6 connections on average. Short bursts filled the pool and caused subsequent lookups to wait.

Before adding a cache, the engineers examined which records were being read. Customers repeatedly requested the same popular products, while descriptions, categories, and image references changed infrequently. A database result obtained for one customer could therefore serve several others.

Reusing results reduces the number of source reads. A cache offers less benefit when most requests access a different record, when entries are too large to retain, or when the underlying value changes before another caller can use it. A 90 percent hit rate across Baodium’s three lookup classes would reduce the usual database rate from 3,600 reads per second to about 360. That estimate gives us a useful way to evaluate the proposal: how many source reads would actually disappear? The scope matters. Caching product descriptions does not remove category queries, and a high hit rate for image references says little about price lookups. Measurements need to follow the data classes used by the page.

Cache Eligibility and Freshness

Suppose a merchant changes a product description. A customer who sees the previous wording for a short period may still be able to browse and purchase correctly. The same tolerance cannot automatically be applied to every field on the page.

The permitted age of a cached value depends on how the application uses it. An older description may be acceptable for browsing until the next refresh. Using an outdated price or permission to authorize a purchase can produce an incorrect business decision, so those checks must use a source with the required authority and freshness.

A cached inventory count, for instance, may indicate that an item is available even though another customer has reserved the final unit. A browsing price may also differ from the amount checkout is prepared to authorize. The decision the caller makes with the cached value determines where an older copy is acceptable and where the application needs current authoritative state.

Cache eligibility depends on how the returned value is used.
Data Cached use Required check
Product description Browsing copy with an accepted update delay. Refresh or invalidate after edits.
Image content Reuse under a content-specific URL. Changed content receives a new URL.
Display price Browsing price under a freshness policy. Validate the purchase price before authorization.
Inventory count Availability indication while browsing. Reserve through Inventory Service at purchase.
Payment outcome A view of the recorded payment operation. Resolve uncertainty through the owning service.

Price validation needs a customer-facing rule too. If checkout obtains an updated amount, it must present that amount and obtain any required confirmation before payment. Otherwise, an authoritative read can still lead to a surprising purchase experience.

Some catalog changes require stricter handling than ordinary edits. A product withdrawal or access restriction may need an authoritative check or a separate update mechanism with a tighter freshness requirement. Grouping those controls with descriptive text under one TTL would conceal an important difference in their consequences.

Baodium began with browsing metadata whose update delay was acceptable. PostgreSQL stored the authoritative records, while checkout continued using the services responsible for price validation, reservation, and payment.

The Cache-Aside Read Path

The Catalog team selected a shared Redis cache so one application instance could reuse a value loaded by another. Product Page Service queried Redis first. If the entry was absent, it read PostgreSQL and stored the result for subsequent callers. Figure Figure traces the path a read takes.

This is the cache-aside pattern: the application checks the cache, reads the source on a miss, and populates the cache under its freshness rules.

The read sequence is small, but several decisions are hidden inside it. Can another request load the same missing key? What happens if the cache write fails? Could the database record change between the read and cache population? We will work through those cases before treating this as a production implementation.

Cache Keys and Representations

A cache key identifies the result being reused, and it must include every input that can change that result. If a product description depends on language, a key containing only the product ID can return the wrong language. If prices depend on currency or customer group, those inputs belong in the price key. Customer-specific data stored under a shared key can also be disclosed to another customer.

Authorization still applies before returning protected data, even when the value is already cached.

The example includes a representation version, v1. A new namespace can prevent an incompatible deployment from reading values serialized by earlier code. It also causes misses for the new namespace, which must be included in the rollout plan.

Key design affects invalidation as well. When one product has several language or currency variants, an update needs to identify which cached representations are affected. A key scheme that is easy to construct but difficult to invalidate creates work elsewhere in the application.

Cache Placement

A shared cache introduces a network call but allows reuse across application instances. An in-process cache avoids that call, while giving each process its own contents, memory allocation, and restart behavior.

A CDN is useful for public content such as product images. Using a URL derived from the image’s content allows the old URL to continue identifying the old image, while an updated page refers to the new URL. Mutable image references on the page still need their own refresh policy.

These placements can be combined, but every copy adds another place where an earlier value may be served. A five-minute application TTL does not bound the total age of a response that another layer caches afterward. For Baodium’s initial metadata cache, a shared store avoided introducing another independently refreshed copy in every process. Local caching could be added later if measurements showed that particular keys justified it.

Expiration and Data Age

Baodium allowed ordinary browsing metadata to be cached for five minutes. The time to live, or TTL, determined how long an entry could be reused after it was stored. The TTL limits reuse after the cache write; it does not limit the value’s age. That age also depends on what happened before the cache write. A loader reads an older database version, pauses, and eventually stores it with a fresh five-minute TTL. The value’s age includes the pause as well as its time in Redis. Reading from a delayed replica can add age before the loader even receives the result.

TTL therefore needs to be interpreted alongside the source-read policy. Strict age requirements may require source-version information, validation time, bounded loader duration, and a rule for rejecting results that arrive after their validation is no longer acceptable.

For ordinary browsing metadata, Baodium used expiration alongside invalidation after updates. Invalidation reduced the usual update delay, while expiration caused a later reload if an invalidation was delayed.

TTL selection also changes database work, because short expiration intervals increase refresh reads. Large intervals improve reuse but permit an unchanged cached entry to be served for more time. The product’s freshness requirement and measured reuse determine whether that trade-off is useful.

Source Updates and Cache Invalidation

Suppose a merchant changes a description and PostgreSQL commits the new version. Redis may still contain the previous description, so the write path needs to update or invalidate that copy. The two figures below show why the update path needs as much thought as the read path.

Updating Redis after the database commit can reduce the delay before readers see the new value. However, these are separate writes. The process can stop between them, and concurrent writers can finish their cache updates out of source-version order.

The team could rely on entry expiry or add an invalidation path after source updates. The permitted update delay determined which was sufficient.

With expiry alone, a reader reloads an entry after its lifetime ends. The TTL limits reuse after storage. A value loaded from a lagging replica may already be old, and a delayed loader can store an earlier version after a source update. Section Section explains the resulting freshness limit. This option avoids invalidation delivery and ordering, but the full source-update-to-read delay must fit the field’s freshness requirement.

The second position is to invalidate or update the cache when the source changes. In the ordinary case a reader sees the new value soon after the commit, and the interval is set by however long the invalidation takes to arrive rather than by the lifetime. In exchange, correctness now depends on delivery, on ordering between concurrent writers, and on what happens when the commit succeeds and the invalidation is lost. Those are the races the rest of this section examines, and the version metadata described below exists to make them recoverable.

For browsing data that tolerates a documented update delay, I would begin with expiry and measure the full delay under concurrent updates. If that exceeds the requirement, add invalidation or choose another read path. Purchase prices, inventory reservations, and permissions still need authoritative checks when the action is taken, as described in Section Section.

Invalidation removes the copy so another reader can reload it. This avoids populating values that may never be requested again, but still requires reliable handling of every source-update path. At Baodium, merchants were not the only writers; imports, scheduled promotions, supplier feeds, and support tools also changed catalog records. Adding invalidation only to the merchant portal would leave those other changes dependent on expiration.

The Catalog team recorded an invalidation event with each participating source update, using the outbox introduced in Chapter 3.

This transaction records the obligation to invalidate. Readers can still obtain the earlier copy while the event waits for publication or processing. Every writer must participate in this procedure or an equivalent change-capture mechanism. An outbox in the Catalog application cannot account for direct database writes made by a separate import tool.

The consumer also needs to understand cached dependencies. Changing a product’s category may affect its detail entry and one or more category pages. Invalidating only the detail entry can leave the browsing paths inconsistent.

Overlapping Reads and Writes

Even reliable event delivery does not resolve every invalidation race. Consider a reader whose database result arrives just before a source update. A busy catalog serves enough reads and writes that a race requiring a particular ordering within a few milliseconds occurs several times a day.

  1. A reader misses the cache and reads product version 10.

  2. A writer commits version 11.

  3. The version 11 invalidation removes the cached entry.

  4. The delayed reader stores version 10 with a new TTL.

The invalidation was processed, yet the cache contains the old version again. Deleting a key cannot prevent a loader already in progress from recreating it. Where this race mattered, Baodium associated the entry with a minimum accepted source version, often called a version watermark. Processing the version 11 event advanced that minimum to at least 11 and removed any older payload. A population operation compared its source version with the minimum and any existing payload version before writing. The comparison and write were atomic, so a concurrent loader could not insert an older value between the check and the update. A version 10 population was then rejected. A delayed version 10 invalidation event also could not reduce the minimum or remove a version 11 payload. Every population path had to use this rule, including miss loaders, refreshers, and warmers. One unguarded cache write would reintroduce the race.

The requesting handler also needed to inspect the population result. If its version 10 value was rejected because version 11 was already known, it could retrieve an acceptable cached copy, perform a bounded source reload, or return unavailable. Returning version 10 without examining the rejection would bypass the freshness decision for that caller.

Version Metadata and Recovery

Version validation provides a specific guarantee: it rejects populations older than the versions the cache has already recorded. Before the version 11 event arrives, version 10 may still be accepted. The metadata also needs to survive for the period in which older loaders can finish. If eviction, expiration, or a restart removes it, an old loader may write into an apparently empty cache.

A design relying on this protection must define metadata retention and cache-reset behavior. One approach uses a cache generation that loaders capture before reading the source. After a reset, populations from an earlier generation are rejected, and the generation itself requires reliable management.

Use this coordination when rejecting older cache populations is required by the caller’s freshness policy. Ordinary descriptions may tolerate a documented update delay. Current purchase decisions are better served by the authoritative price and inventory procedures already established.

Concurrent Misses and Refresh Work

Now consider concurrent reads of a popular product as its cache entry expires. Figure Figure shows the moment of expiry.

Several requests may observe the miss before any loader stores a result, and each then issues the same database read. This burst is often called a cache stampede, and the picture is a herd that all runs for the same gap in the fence at once. It can happen while the overall hit rate still looks healthy, because the hit rate averages over every key and the stampede involves only one.

Request coalescing allows callers for the same missing key to share a loader. Inside a process, the first caller starts the load and subsequent callers await its result. The loader checks the cache again after obtaining responsibility for the key. Another request may have populated it between the original miss and that point. Waiting callers still need deadlines, and the application must bound the number of loaders and waiters. Otherwise, coalescing reduces duplicate database reads while allowing an excessive number of waiting requests.

Cancellation needs care too. One caller abandoning the page should not automatically cancel a shared load needed by other callers. The coalescing implementation therefore needs its own bounded loader lifetime and separate waiter lifetimes.

Per-process coalescing leaves some duplication across instances; twenty processes may issue twenty source reads for the same key. If the database can accept that burst, a shared coordination mechanism may add more complexity than benefit.

For expensive loads, a refresh lease can coordinate instances. It needs an owner token and expiry, and release must atomically verify the token. A worker whose lease expired must not delete a replacement worker’s lease.

A lease reduces duplicate work but can expire while a loader is still executing. Source-version checks address stale population, and database admission bounds the work if duplicate loads occur.

Expiration Distribution

Coalescing helps with one popular key. A bulk load can create a different problem by assigning similar expiration times to thousands of keys. When those entries expire together, many independent loaders reach the database. Baodium spread ordinary metadata expiration across a range below the maximum accepted TTL, a technique known as TTL jitter. The upper bound must respect the freshness policy. If the maximum permitted interval is five minutes, jitter cannot extend it to six. This spreads refresh work across keys. Requests for one expired key still need the coalescing and admission rules described above.

Serving a Copy During Refresh

For data whose freshness policy permits it, refreshing can begin before the cached copy becomes unusable. The entry has a refresh time and a later final expiry. After the refresh time, one loader obtains a new value while other callers use the accepted copy. After final expiry, callers must reload or receive a permitted degraded result.

This is commonly called stale-while-revalidate. It is useful for browsing metadata because callers do not all need to wait during an ordinary refresh. A failed refresh must not repeatedly extend final expiry. The application also needs bounded background refresh work, especially when many entries become eligible at the same time.

Confirmed Absence and Negative Entries

Absence is a result too, and deciding whether to cache it is trickier than it first appears.

A missing product can generate repeated reads too. If every request for the same invalid ID reaches PostgreSQL, the application repeats an answer it already obtained. A short negative-cache entry records confirmed absence. It needs a distinct representation such as NOT_FOUND, so the reader can distinguish it from a cache miss or an empty product. Only an authoritative missing-record result may create that entry; a timeout or connection failure leaves the result unknown. Caching it as absence would turn a temporary outage into a false product-not-found response.

Product creation and restoration must also invalidate or supersede negative entries; otherwise, a newly available product can appear missing until expiration.

Negative caching helps when callers repeat the same absent identifiers. A stream of unique invalid IDs still creates misses, so source admission must apply to this path as well.

Decision review

The cache cluster has just failed over

Product Page Service handles about 1,200 page requests per second, and each page needs three catalog reads. The cache was answering 90 percent of them. A failover has left the cache empty but reachable, and PostgreSQL is now receiving close to 3,600 reads per second instead of 360. Acquisition waits are climbing and pages are timing out.

Warm the cache by looping over the most requested products as fast as the loader allows.

Bound how many concurrent misses may reach the database, let the rest wait or fail, and warm a small set first.

Bypass the cache entirely until the incident is over, so reads go straight to PostgreSQL without the extra hop.

C bypasses the cache and sends every read to the source. It therefore removes the reduction in database reads that recovery depends on. Every read goes to the database at ten times the rate it was sized for, and the situation persists until traffic falls.

A is the instinct that turns a cache failure into a database outage. A warmer running flat out competes with live traffic for the same connections, so the queue that live requests are waiting in gets longer while the warmer runs.

B is the recovery this chapter argues for, and the order matters. Bound the database’s concurrency first, so the source survives whatever the cache does. Then warm a small set of popular keys under that bound, since a handful of products account for most reads during a promotion. Requests that cannot be served fall back to a reduced page rather than waiting. The cost is that some customers see an incomplete page for a few minutes, while admitted requests continue completing within the tested database allocation.

Cold Caches and Cache Failure

Once most reads are served from the cache, losing those hits can change database demand substantially. At a 90 percent hit rate, a complete cache outage can send approximately ten times the usual source-read rate toward PostgreSQL. If you provision PostgreSQL for the usual miss rate, a cache outage tests a different workload: ten source reads for every one it normally receives. Measure whether the database can serve that rate before allowing unrestricted fallback. That condition does not require a connection error. An empty replacement cache, a namespace change, or widespread eviction can produce ordinary misses with the same consequence. The database admission check therefore belongs on every source-read path; placing it only in the cache-error handler leaves these other cases unbounded.

A slow cache needs a short call deadline as well. Without one, a request can spend most of its budget waiting for Redis before attempting PostgreSQL. During an observed outage, the application may temporarily bypass cache calls, while continuing to enforce source admission.

The following examples bring these decisions into the read path; the helper APIs are illustrative and include the population rules discussed earlier.

The initial lookup uses the caller’s cache deadline. After a miss, singleflight.run coalesces concurrent requests for the same key and invokes a loader with its own bounded context. The loader then checks the cache again before consuming database capacity.

The coalescing helper creates a bounded loader context separate from any individual waiter’s deadline. The cache helpers return explicit outcomes for missing entries, unavailable cache access, and rejected populations. A failed cache write does not invalidate a successful source read, so that result can still be returned. A version rejection means newer evidence is already known and needs separate handling, and this example returns temporary unavailability instead of starting another read.

The database permit covers the source operation through local cleanup. Warmers, refreshers, and verification reads also use the source allocation, rather than each receiving an independent allowance against the same database. The combined allocation must fit local connection pools and the database workload across the fleet. Static instance shares need to include rollout overlap. Dynamically allocated shares need defined behavior when an allocation expires or its controller cannot be reached.

Warming and Recovery

A shared cache does not become empty when one application instance restarts. Warming is relevant after a cache reset, namespace change, or the creation of a separate local cache. Baodium warmed a selected set of frequently requested keys at a bounded rate. Loading the entire catalog would use database reads and memory for products that might never be requested. Warmers shared the source allowance with live misses and could be paused when customer requests needed that capacity, and their entries also used distributed expiration times.

The recovery test included both warming and live requests. Filling the cache as fast as possible could reproduce the database overload that the cache was intended to prevent.

Field note

Facebook, September 2010

Facebook’s September 2010 outage lasted about two and a half hours. A configuration-repair mechanism treated a changed persistent value as invalid. Clients repeatedly queried the backing databases to repair it, producing hundreds of thousands of queries per second. Database errors then caused clients to delete cached entries, which generated further queries even after the original value was corrected.

Engineers stopped traffic to the database cluster, disabled the repair mechanism, and restored traffic gradually. A repair path needs admission control just as an ordinary cache-miss path does. An unavailable source also supplies no basis for replacing a cached value with a negative entry.

Source: published incident report.

Memory and Popular Keys

A cache can answer every request successfully while removing very few reads from the source database.

A cache can be reachable while providing poor reuse because entries are evicted before their TTL expires. When memory fills, the eviction policy determines which entries are removed. A policy based on recent access may respond well to changing demand, but a catalog scan can introduce many one-use records. A frequency-based policy may retain established popular entries while reacting less readily to a new promotion.

The choice needs testing against the application’s access pattern. Source-read rate, hit rate, evictions, and memory use explain the result better than the policy name alone. Memory estimates should include serialized payloads and metadata overhead. Caching an entire product response when callers reuse only a small portion may waste both memory and transfer time.

A single popular key can also concentrate requests on its owning shard. Adding shards does not automatically distribute that key’s reads; per-shard measurements are therefore necessary when aggregate cache metrics appear satisfactory.

A small local cache may reduce repeated network reads for such a key when its freshness policy allows another copy. That is a measured extension to the design, with its own expiration and invalidation requirements.

Verification and Production Measurements

The release tests needed to answer two questions: how much source work was avoided, and whether the returned copies satisfied their intended use. For the read path, the engineers tested an empty cache, a timed-out cache, concurrent requests for an expired product, and many entries expiring together. Source admission had to apply in every case, including when Redis returned ordinary misses.

For the update path, they paused a loader after it read an old version, committed a source update, processed invalidation, and then allowed the loader to finish. This reproduced the population race that a sequential read-write test would miss. They also tested delayed invalidation, cache resets during loading, creation after a negative entry, and recovery while customers continued browsing.

In production, source reads per second showed the database work still occurring. Hit rate by route and data class identified where reuse was effective. Coalesced requests, refreshes, and admission rejections explained what happened after misses.

Cache latency, errors, memory, and evictions were measured per shard, while invalidation lag and sampled source-version comparisons provided evidence about freshness. Sampling itself used a bounded database allocation. A difference immediately after an update could be permitted by the freshness policy, so a mismatch count alone could not call it a defect. Any repair also needed concurrency protection. A verifier that observed an old entry could not blindly delete the key after another caller had populated a newer value. Repair used a conditional version check or the normal invalidation procedure.

Finally, the page response preserved the distinction between absence and unavailability; optional metadata could be omitted after an admission rejection. A product-not-found result required confirmed absence, and checkout still obtained the authoritative decisions needed for purchase.

Summary

Caching reduced the number of catalog reads Baodium sent to its database, especially when many customers requested the same product during a promotion. That improvement depended on which source changes made a cached entry obsolete and how the application handled requests when no usable entry existed.

Three cases deserve separate tests. A read that overlaps a merchant update can repopulate the cache with an older version unless invalidation and population follow a compatible ordering rule. Concurrent cache misses can send more database work than the source can complete. During a cache outage, every attempted fallback to the database competes for the same finite capacity. Expiration, source versions, coordinated loading, and bounded source admission address different portions of those failure paths; none can substitute for an authoritative check when a purchase depends on current price, inventory, or permissions.

The team chose the cache’s behavior from the acceptable age of each result, then checked the work required to restore the cache after failure. The next chapter moves from reusable data to the application process itself: reproducing a tested binary and its dependencies on another host does not by itself reproduce its resource limits, configuration, or behavior during startup and shutdown.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & The selected browsing data permits a defined update delay, and reusing frequently requested records reduces source reads by the measured hit rate.
Condition that tests it & A popular entry expires, an invalidation is missed, or the cache becomes unavailable.
Constraint or invariant & Cache calls, concurrent loaders, database connections, and source-read admission have separate limits. Live misses, refreshers, warmers, and verification share the database allocation.
Evidence and uncertainty & The usual product-page workload generated 3,600 database reads per second per affected instance. A 90 percent hit rate across those lookups would reduce source reads to about 360 per second, before refresh and verification work.

The miss rate during expiration, eviction, or cache loss, and whether delayed populations can violate the accepted freshness policy after updates or cache resets.
Signal and evaluation window & During cache-loss and refresh tests, measure source-read concurrency, cache age, and acquisition time.
Control and decision & Use cached copies under their freshness policy and apply source admission to every miss path. Preserve the difference between missing data and unavailable data, and validate purchase decisions through their authoritative services.
Owner and review trigger & The Catalog owner defines cache eligibility and update handling. The service and database owners agree on source-read admission and recovery capacity. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.
